content: 1. HIV Case Surveillance and Reporting Systems HIV case surveillance systems have been implemented in various countries to monitor the epidemic and improve patient care. These systems collect data on new HIV diagnoses, including demographic information, risk factors, and clinical outcomes. For example, in Haiti, an HIV case-reporting system has been in place since 2010. It records the date and location of diagnosis, patient demographics, self-reported risk factors, and clinical outcomes such as ART initiation, CD4 test results, and WHO clinical staging. This system enables the identification of service gaps and tracks patient mobility and retention in care. Similarly, El Salvador has developed a fully digitized HIV surveillance system called SUMEVE, which collects data on individuals with positive HIV test results, clinical follow-up, and ARV prescriptions. Between 2015 and 2016, the system was enhanced to identify gaps in care and treatment quality at the health center and provincial levels. 2. Use of Unique Identifiers in HIV Monitoring Unique identifiers are alphanumeric codes assigned to individuals to ensure accurate and repeated identification across health services. These identifiers are anonymous and linked to a secure database containing personal information. The use of unique identifiers facilitates the transition from service-centered to person-centered data, improving care quality and supporting data linkages as patients move between facilities and geographic locations. Unique identifiers also help de-duplicate testing data, improve retention in care, and ensure confidentiality and security of health information. They are critical for linking HIV services with broader health systems and for tracking clinical outcomes over time. 3. Monitoring the Dynamics of the HIV Epidemic Surveillance systems use assays for recent infection and serotyping to monitor the dynamics of the HIV epidemic. For instance, in France, these methods have been employed to track new HIV diagnoses and assess transmission patterns. Data collected through these systems provide insights into the geographical distribution of HIV cases, prevalence among key populations, and the effectiveness of prevention and treatment programs. 4. Geographical Prioritization of HIV Interventions Countries like Myanmar have used HIV case data to estimate resource needs and prioritize interventions based on the burden of HIV and the risk of new infections. Townships are categorized as high, medium, or low priority based on variables such as population size, HIV prevalence, and the availability of ART services. This approach allows targeted interventions in high-risk areas, such as border regions, economic zones, and locations with significant migrant populations. 5. Improving Data Systems and Interoperability Transitioning from paper-based to electronic patient information systems is essential for improving data quality and program efficiency. Countries are encouraged to invest in robust and secure data systems that support interoperability and adopt open-source standards. WHO recommends allocating 5–10% of the program budget to strengthen monitoring and evaluation systems. 6. Data Quality and Use for Program Improvement Periodic reviews of patient monitoring systems are necessary to assess data quality and improve care. Facility-level indicators, such as early warning signs for HIV drug resistance, should be collected to monitor and enhance service delivery. Longitudinal data can be used to track clinical outcomes, analyze care cascades, and identify gaps in linkage to care and retention. 7. Key Population Data and Confidentiality Data on key populations, such as injection drug users and men who have sex with men, must be collected with strict confidentiality and security measures. Patient records should not include key population categories unless necessary for patient management and referral. WHO provides guidance on addressing confidentiality issues and ensuring that data collection supports program improvement without compromising patient privacy. 8. Benefits and Risks of Unique Identifiers Unique identifiers improve continuity of care, facilitate easier transfer of treatment between facilities, and enhance the linkage of HIV and health services. They also support better management of drug stocks and diagnostics, improve planning, and ensure data security. However, the implementation of unique identifiers requires careful consideration of system complexity and the balance between benefits and risks. 9. Person-Centered Monitoring in the Treat All Approach The treat all approach, which ensures that all individuals living with HIV receive ART, requires robust monitoring systems to track patient progress and service delivery. Unique identifiers play a crucial role in linking health facility and community monitoring systems, ensuring continuity of care, and supporting differentiated care models. 10. Types of Unique Identifiers Unique identifiers can be implemented at different levels, such as facility, program, or national levels. The complexity of the system increases with the level of implementation, but so do the benefits, such as improved data linkage and program efficiency.
